title: When Locking People Up Is the Local Jobs Plan
hook: Rural places have sold prison beds to distant governments since the 1800s. Immigration detention has revived the trade — and with it an economy that grows only when enforcement does.
key_points: Sociologist Ella Siegrist argues federal payments for housing prisoners have long functioned as rural economic development.
West Virginia took federal and D.C. prisoners starting in 1876; its prison population went from about 160 to over 1,200 by 1908.
Those payments reached roughly $77,000 over two years by 1908 — about $2.8 million today — and the system shrank once federal penitentiaries opened.
The modern version is the per-diem contract: ICE pays a daily rate per detainee, reported at $291 in one Indiana facility and $90 in West Virginia.
ICE detention grew 58% between 2025 and 2026, accounting for effectively all recent growth in U.S. incarceration.
The structural problem is incentive: a locality funded per occupied bed benefits from more enforcement, whatever the policy merits.
content_html: Prisons are usually argued about as criminal justice policy. Writing in The Conversation, sociologist Ella Siegrist makes the case that in rural America they have also long been a fiscal strategy: a way for a cash-poor county or state to import revenue by housing someone else's prisoners.
extra_html:
Her historical example is West Virginia, which from 1876 accepted federal and Washington, D.C. prisoners to relieve crowded urban facilities. Its prison population climbed from roughly 160 to more than 1,200 by 1908, when the payments reached about $77,000 over two years — near $2.8 million in today's money. When federal penitentiaries opened at Atlanta and Leavenworth, the revenue stopped and the system shrank, which is the tell: the growth had tracked the money, not local crime.

Immigration detention has restored the trade in a modern form. ICE pays a daily rate per detainee — reported at $291 at one Indiana facility, $90 in West Virginia — and closed or half-empty facilities are reopening on that promise, with officials citing job counts. Siegrist notes ICE detention rose 58% between 2025 and 2026, accounting for essentially all recent growth in U.S. incarceration. The result is a category of local economy whose revenue rises only when enforcement does, which is a difficult thing to unwind once towns are counting on it.

related.title: When Detention Is a Revenue Line
related.hook: Contract out a coercive government function and you create a company whose earnings rise with enforcement — and whose shareholders now have a stake in how the policy goes.

related.title: Strings Attached: When Federal Money Becomes Leverage
related.hook: A national government that can't order regions around directly can often get the same result by attaching conditions to its money — which is why courts ask where persuasion ends and coercion begins.

related.title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
related.hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'

flashcards.prompt: How does a per-diem detention contract shape a local government's incentives?
flashcards.back_html: Revenue arrives per occupied bed per day, so the locality's budget improves when detention rises — a financial stake in enforcement levels that is independent of whether the policy is sound.

flashcards.prompt: What happened to West Virginia's prison system after federal penitentiaries opened around 1908?

choices.text: It contracted, because the federal payments it depended on dried up
It kept expanding on state funding alone
It was taken over and run directly by the federal government

flashcards.explanation_html: The growth had been driven by payments for housing outside prisoners. When that revenue stream ended, the system shrank with it.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Siegrist call these facilities a form of public works rather than economic development?
flashcards.back_html: The jobs exist only as long as another government keeps paying to fill the beds. Nothing durable is built locally, so the community stays dependent on the flow of outside enforcement money.
